pr_title: Refactor root-level serialization logic and polymorphic value handling.
pr_body:
Refactors the root-level serialization/deserialization routines so that

1. Both `JsonSerializerOptions` and `JsonTypeInfo<T>` overloads in `JsonSerializer` call into common helper methods, ensuring that metadata is being handled consistently regardless of invoked overload.
2. Polymorphic handling of root-level `object` values is moved to the converter layer. Fixes #72187 and #72681.

It must be noted that this change introduces a slight performance regression, specifically when it comes to serializing small root-level `object` values:

### [System.Text.Json.Serialization.Tests.WriteJson<Int32>.SerializeObjectProperty](https://github.com/dotnet/performance/blob/945eb2a8ae39f3692885e1029d0cda9d3d249954/src/benchmarks/micro/libraries/System.Text.Json/Serializer/WriteJson.cs#L69)

|                  Method |        Job |                                                                                                         Toolchain |     Mean |   Error |   StdDev |   Median |      Min |      Max | Ratio | MannWhitney(3%) | RatioSD |  Gen 0 | Allocated | Alloc Ratio |
|------------------------ |----------- |------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |---------:|--------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|------:|---------------- |--------:|-------:|----------:|------------:|
| SerializeObjectProperty | Job-LSKJVH |        main | 235.7 ns | 5.44 ns |  5.82 ns | 236.1 ns | 226.0 ns | 246.8 ns |  1.00 |            Base |    0.00 | 0.0254 |     264 B |        1.00 |
| SerializeObjectProperty | Job-KLBYHL | PR | 249.3 ns | 8.82 ns | 10.16 ns | 249.8 ns | 231.8 ns | 270.1 ns |  1.06 |          Slower |    0.04 | 0.0260 |     264 B |        1.00 |

Fundamentally, it is caused by this change removing the hardcoded polymorphic serialization for root-level `object` values. Instead of directly resolving the metadata for the runtime type, the metadata for `object` is consulted _before_ proceeding with polymorphic serialization. As such, in the worst-case scenario, two lookups need to be made against the metadata cache instead of just one.

I've been able to recover some of the performance losses by [employing a secondary LRU cache](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72789/commits/80a1fa9bd484bc2276d131e49a5b1ea239e2df54#diff-e9ac53ab9e93a974203023f17f11923b1a4c4e8cf38c28ae0bbee95a030a0620R25) specifically used for root-level polymorphic types. I think we should merge this PR and accept the performance regression, as it is essential for getting https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/72187 and https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/72681 fixed. The performance regression only impacts small, root-level polymorphic values and does not affect the statically typed APIs or the source generator which are more performance-minded.

cc @jeffhandley @steveharter @ericstj

If incorrect code or code wrote under wrong assumptions is faster then there is no perf regression to me. We should baseline from correct code. If there are any quick wins to gain the perf back then even better

I made a few tweaks to the caching strategy in 97a8b7a53ffae83e3ae30b9f2cb9d938896b0d44, caching the resolved `JsonTypeInfo<object>` instead of using a secondary LRU cache for polymorphic types, which has contributed to even more performance gains:

|                  Method |        Job |                                                                                                         Toolchain |     Mean |    Error |   StdDev |   Median |      Min |      Max | Ratio | MannWhitney(3%) | RatioSD |  Gen 0 | Allocated | Alloc Ratio |
|------------------------ |----------- |------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|------:|---------------- |--------:|-------:|----------:|------------:|
| SerializeObjectProperty | Job-LZOHNV |  main | 257.1 ns | 10.66 ns | 11.85 ns | 259.2 ns | 238.0 ns | 281.6 ns |  1.00 |            Base |    0.00 | 0.0261 |     264 B |        1.00 |
| SerializeObjectProperty | Job-RKZQDC | PR | 268.1 ns |  7.07 ns |  7.85 ns | 268.3 ns | 247.5 ns | 279.9 ns |  1.05 |            Same |    0.06 | 0.0258 |     264 B |        1.00 |

review_comments: can we get this from PropertyInfoForTypeInfo?
Possibly, but I think we should look at eventually removing `PropertyInfoForTypeInfo` in the future.
I assume we're not calling this with i.e. customized converters?
You mean `CustomConverter` from `JsonPropertyInfo`? No, it doesn't apply to root values.
Consider changing `CanUseSerializationLogic` so it's always false for polimorphic types (I hope you can eliminate the check for `ContainsMetadata`).

`CanUseSerializationLogic` is scoped to `JsonSerializerOptions`, whereas polymorphism is scoped to the individual types being serialized on the current stack. The same holds for `ContainsMetadata` which is dynamic and reflects whether the current value is writing any `$metadata` properties on the wire.
are we not adding `&& options.CanUseFor...`?
`options` can still be mutable at this stage, so this is deferred for the configure stage.

actually previous logic made more sense to me because we disposed of the writer earlier so it was clear that `output.WrittenMemory.ToArray()` converted all bytes. With this specific usage I expect in some cases we might not convert something (i.e. closing brace etc.)

The `WriteCore` methods all do flushing of their own, so even though the sequence of disposal changes somewhat, it only concerns clearing state and returning buffers without any real functional impact.

This PR removes the distinction between "generated serializer" and "serializer" entrypoints, since the introduction of custom contract resolvers has made it obsolete. The helper methods are replaced with typed and untyped JsonTypeInfo variants.
Changes to testing in line with the recommendations put out in #72681.
I assume this is the actual change for being more consistent with polymorphism?
Correct, we no longer consult the runtime type here, it becomes the responsibility of the converter.
isn't it better to have this just in ReadFromSpan or rather closer to wherever it needs to be configured? (assuming it's not already there) - I'd avoid adding to in any "proxy" methods

For source JsonTypeInfo sources like the `JsonSerializerOptions` cache it is already guaranteed for the value to be configured. Which is why we only need to do this in public methods that accept `JsonTypeInfo<T>`. I've replaced the `EnsureConfigured()` calls with asserts to make sure nothing slips.
Did we actually hit any issue with these? I'm surprised none of the tests failed. Aren't we configuring in `ReadDocument` or futher?
same question for other EnsureConfigured

> Did we actually hit any issue with these? I'm surprised none of the tests failed. Aren't we configuring in ReadDocument or futher?

We did, that's what #72630 was fixing. `EnsureConfigured()` will eventually get called but only on an on-demand basis. This ensures that the value is locked as soon as it is passed to the serializer.
similar comment here - I'd expect writer to be disposed after `WriteCoreAsObject` - otherwise I can't safely tell if we wrote entire input
(also if there are any exceptions they'd happen in more logical place)
See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72789/files/b912c81b3a81ae30a46a3b4e42c9351eb3920998#r929785869. Flushing is handled by the `WriteCore` methods.
Added for consistency with the `JsonConverter.WriteCoreAsObject` method.
`!` after `SerializeHandler` should not be required because of the assert. If it is for whatever reason you can also put `MemberNotNullWhen` on CanUseSerializeHandler
It's not smart enough to recognize that the separate downcast inside the assert is the same as this one. I suppose a `MemberNotNull` would fix it, but this is really the only place we're using it.
On second thought `MemberNotNull` would not address the problem either, since we check the property in the base variable.
I'm curious - could user possibly write type discriminators for `JsonTypeInfo<object>` and expect them to be deserialized directly rather than through JsonNode?
Possibly -- although that would end up using the type system directly rather than a pure DOM. That being said, type discriminators on `object` are explicitly prohibited for the moment.
